title: Track 1, Lesson 3: Risk tolerance - how much volatility can you actually take?
subtitle: Investing well is not picking the highest-returning asset, but picking the one you can live with when it falls.
whyItMatters: A great many people abandon investing halfway through, not because they picked the wrong asset but because they picked one beyond what they could psychologically bear. This lesson helps you establish your risk tolerance BEFORE investing, so you don't panic-sell when markets move.
openingQuestion: Your portfolio falls 20% in a month. What do you do?
openingOptions: Nothing at all, because you don't want to open the app and look
Go back to the risk tolerance you assessed beforehand
Borrow from several sources to recover the loss as fast as possible
Sell everything to 'cut losses', though the plan was to hold long term
explanation: Risk tolerance has to be established BEFORE investing, not while the market is falling. If you chose a portfolio that genuinely matches what you can bear, a 20% fall should not be a reason to panic-sell - unless the original risk assessment was wrong.

diagram.label: Financial capacity: how much can you lose and still be fine
Psychological capacity: how far a fall costs you sleep
Take the lower of the two as your limit
Choose a portfolio inside that limit - before markets move

realWorldExample.description: Many new investors sell out at the bottom during sharp falls because they never anticipated the swings - they chose a portfolio riskier than their real psychological capacity, and then panicked at exactly the wrong moment.

quiz.question: What determines your risk tolerance?
options: Both your financial capacity and your psychological capacity
Only how volatile the market happens to be now
Only financial capacity, with psychology excluded
Only the current balance of your investment account
quiz.explanation: Risk tolerance = FINANCIAL capacity + PSYCHOLOGICAL capacity. The two can differ: someone may have enough money to absorb a loss (good financial capacity) but lose sleep worrying (poor psychological capacity) - and should hold a more cautious portfolio even though 'on paper' they could take more risk.

quiz.question: Why is a young person with stable income and no family usually advised to take more risk than someone near retirement?
options: Because shares always rise within the first 5 years of investing
Because a young person has a long time to recover from a fall
Because young people receive preferential trading fees
Because young people always understand investing better
quiz.explanation: The time horizon is part of financial capacity. A young person has decades for the portfolio to recover from a downturn, while someone near retirement needs to draw on the money soon and cannot wait for markets to come back after a shock.

quiz.question: Two people each have 500 million to invest. A sleeps soundly through a 30% fall. B loses sleep at a 5% fall. Who should hold the riskier portfolio (more shares)?
options: Neither of them should hold a high-risk portfolio
B, because being cautious means they will research more carefully
Both equally, since they each have 500 million to invest
A, whose psychological capacity is higher
quiz.explanation: Psychological capacity is an axis independent of money or age. A can take 30% of volatility without panicking and suits a riskier portfolio (more shares); B should hold something more cautious despite the same capital, to avoid selling at the wrong moment when markets move.

quiz.question: Someone has very high financial capacity to absorb losses but loses sleep when the portfolio falls 15%. Which axis should set the portfolio?
options: Financial capacity, since the emotions settle after a few cycles
Financial capacity, since it is the constraint you can measure
The average of financial capacity and psychological capacity
The lower of the two, meaning psychological capacity
quiz.explanation: The two axes are constraints that must both be satisfied, so the lower one governs. A portfolio inside financial capacity but beyond psychological capacity gets sold at the bottom - and the loss becomes real rather than staying on paper.

quiz.question: Why establish risk tolerance before markets move rather than while the portfolio is falling?
options: Because in a loss, emotion decides instead of the plan
Because tolerance can only be measured in a calm market
Because brokers require it to be declared at account opening
Because risk tolerance can never be changed once it is set
quiz.explanation: Risk tolerance is a commitment written down while calm, to protect you from yourself while panicking. Measured mid-fall, what you capture is not your capacity to endure but your level of fear at that moment.

keyTakeaways: Risk tolerance = FINANCIAL capacity + PSYCHOLOGICAL capacity; a suitable portfolio has to sit inside both limits
Establish it BEFORE investing, not while markets are moving
A portfolio beyond your psychological capacity leads to selling at the wrong time - doing more harm than good

practicePrompt.question: You build an 80% equity portfolio because the arithmetic says you could absorb a 40% loss without it affecting your life. But when the portfolio falls just 15%, you lose sleep and want to sell everything. What is happening?
options: Risk tolerance covers psychology as well as finances; an 80% equity portfolio is beyond your psychological limit
Nothing is wrong here, because once the financial capacity has been calculated correctly a temporary feeling of anxiety does not matter
You should borrow more money to buy additional shares at the lower price, turning the anxiety into an opportunity for higher returns
This is simply a normal reaction and has nothing whatsoever to do with establishing the risk tolerance that suits you
practicePrompt.explanation: Risk tolerance covers both financial and psychological capacity - a suitable portfolio has to sit inside both limits, not just the financial one.

summary.keyIdea: Risk tolerance = FINANCIAL capacity + PSYCHOLOGICAL capacity; a suitable portfolio has to sit inside both limits
summary.commonMistake: Reading the idea as a phrase to remember rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Establish risk tolerance BEFORE investing, not while markets are moving

application.title: Test yourself
application.message: Picture your portfolio falling 20% in a month - would you want to sell straight away? If so, your current portfolio may be beyond your real risk tolerance.
application.secondary: Answer honestly, not with the answer you think you 'should' give.

sections.text: Investing well is not picking the asset with the highest expected return, but picking the portfolio you can genuinely live with when it falls. Risk tolerance is that boundary - and it has to be established before you put money in, not while the market is dropping and you are casting about for an answer.
The two axes of risk tolerance

Risk tolerance has two independent parts: financial capacity (how much you can lose without it affecting your life) and psychological capacity (how much volatility you can take without losing sleep or panic-selling). The two do not always match: someone may have enough money to absorb a 30% loss (good financial capacity) but lie awake over a 5% fall (poor psychological capacity) - and should hold a more cautious portfolio even though 'on paper' they could take more risk.
The time horizon is part of financial capacity too

A young person with stable income and no family is usually advised to take more risk than someone near retirement - not because they are better at it, but because they have decades for the portfolio to recover from a fall, and no need to draw on the money now. Someone near retirement needs to withdraw soon and cannot wait for markets to recover after a shock - so they need a steadier portfolio, accepting a lower expected return.

left.label: Financial capacity
left.text: How much you could lose without disrupting daily life: depends on income, emergency fund, and the investing time you have left.

right.label: Psychological capacity
right.text: How much volatility you can take without panic-selling: depends on temperament, experience, and how keenly you feel risk.

items: Establish risk tolerance BEFORE putting money in, not once markets are moving
Where financial and psychological capacity conflict, always follow the lower of the two
A 20% fall should not be a reason to panic-sell - unless the original risk assessment was wrong
Revisit your risk tolerance when life circumstances change (marriage, children, approaching retirement)

lines: The best portfolio is not the highest-returning one, but the one you manage to hold through the worst stretches.
